title: What does the research say about silicone scar sheets?
description: A careful look at why silicone sheets appear in scar-care guidance—and where the clinical evidence is still uncertain.
dek: Silicone sheets are widely recommended as a non-invasive scar-care option, but ‘widely recommended’ is not the same as guaranteed results.
takeaways: Clinical guidance commonly includes silicone sheets and gels as a first-line, non-invasive option.
A 2021 Cochrane review found the available trials small and the certainty of evidence low or very low for several outcomes.
Silicone tape belongs on closed, fully healed skin—not an open or weeping wound.

sections.heading: Why silicone appears in scar-care guidance
paragraphs: An international expert review of scar-management guidance describes silicone sheets and gels as a first-line, non-invasive option for both preventing and treating hypertrophic scars and keloids. That recommendation reflects clinical experience, practicality and the body of evidence available at the time.
It does not mean every silicone product has been proven to change every scar. Product quality, the type and age of a scar, wear time and individual skin can all affect a person’s experience.

sections.heading: What the strongest review found
paragraphs: A 2021 Cochrane review examined 13 studies of silicone gel sheeting for hypertrophic scars. The authors found that many studies were small, reported results poorly or carried a high risk of bias.

Their conclusion was deliberately cautious: silicone sheets may help some outcomes, but the evidence was too uncertain to support sweeping promises. That is why responsible scar-care copy should talk about managing scar appearance, not removing scars or guaranteeing a result.

sections.heading: Using sheets as part of a routine
paragraphs: Follow the product instructions and use silicone tape only after a wound has closed and healed. Apply it to clean, dry skin, build wear time gradually and stop if irritation develops.
If a scar is painful, changing quickly, restricting movement or causing concern, ask a qualified healthcare professional for individual advice.

title: Keloid or hypertrophic scar: what’s the difference?
description: The key distinction between two raised scar types, explained without trying to diagnose your skin online.
dek: Both can be raised and firm, but their growth pattern is an important clinical distinction.
takeaways: A hypertrophic scar stays within the boundary of the original injury.
A keloid grows beyond the original wound boundary into nearby skin.
Appearance alone is not always enough for self-diagnosis; seek professional advice if you are unsure.

sections.heading: The boundary is the clearest distinction
paragraphs: Hypertrophic scars and keloids both involve excess scar tissue. The simplest textbook distinction is where that tissue grows: a hypertrophic scar remains within the original wound, while a keloid extends beyond its edges.
Their timing and natural course may also differ. Hypertrophic scars often appear relatively soon after an injury and can gradually settle. Keloids can continue growing and may return after treatment.

sections.heading: Why the difference matters
paragraphs: Treatment choices depend on the scar, its location, symptoms, history and the person’s skin. Reviews describe management as potentially involving several approaches rather than one universal treatment.

That is also why a consumer scar-care product should not promise to remove a keloid. Silicone can be one non-invasive part of scar management, but assessment and treatment planning belong with a qualified professional.

sections.heading: When to ask for help
paragraphs: Consider speaking with a GP, dermatologist or scar specialist if a raised scar is growing beyond the original wound, is painful or itchy, restricts movement, or is affecting your wellbeing.
For routine silicone tape use, wait until the skin is completely closed and healed, and stop if irritation occurs.
